title: Activation Function
body:

---

The fixed squashing function $\sigma$ applied to each [[Neuron]]'s weighted sum. It contributes no
[[Weights]] and is never learned: it is a hyperparameter you choose per layer, and Evan's line
above is the right default, [[ReLU]] on the hidden layers.

$$
y = \sigma(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b)
$$

Two requirements, and they are the whole design space:

1. **[[Non-Linear|Non-linear]]**, or the network collapses to a single linear layer and depth buys
   nothing. This is the only reason the function is there.
2. **Differentiable**, or nearly so, because [[Back Propagation]] has to pass a gradient through
   it. This is what ruled out the [[Perceptron]]'s step function, whose derivative is zero
   everywhere it exists.

## Choosing one

| Function | Range | Use it on | Trouble |
|---|---|---|---|
| step | $\{0,1\}$ | nothing, historical | not differentiable, no gradient |
| [[Sigmoid]] | $(0,1)$ | output, for a probability | saturates, vanishing gradients |
| $\tanh$ | $(-1,1)$ | output, zero-centred alternative | saturates the same way |
| [[ReLU]] | $[0,\infty)$ | **hidden layers, the default** | dead units |
| [[Leaky ReLU]] | $\mathbb{R}$ | hidden layers, when units die | one more constant to pick |
| softmax | simplex | multi-class output | output layer only |

**Hidden layers and the output layer answer to different pressures.** A hidden layer wants a
gradient that survives being multiplied through a deep chain, which is [[ReLU]]'s argument. An
output layer wants its numbers to *mean* something: a probability in $(0,1)$ for
[[Binary Classification]] ([[Sigmoid]]), a distribution over $k$ classes (softmax), or an unbounded
number for regression (no activation at all). See [[Output Layer]].

The derivative is the property that decides everything. [[Sigmoid]]'s peaks at $0.25$, so a chain
of $n$ of them shrinks the gradient by at least $4^{-n}$ and the early layers stop learning;
[[ReLU]]'s is exactly $1$ wherever the unit is active, so nothing shrinks. [[Chain Rule]] in
[[CALCULUS 1]] owns that argument.

## Related

- [[Non-Linear]]: why one is needed at all, with the collapse argument
- [[Neuron]], [[Hidden Layer]], [[Output Layer]]: where it sits
- [[Back Propagation]], [[Chain Rule]]: what it has to be differentiable for
